lines.text: The last topic left you with one uncomfortable fact.
Postgres never changes a row where it sits. An update just writes a new copy and walks away from the old one.
Do that forever, and nothing cleans itself up on its own. Something else has to.
I deleted half the rows in a real table on this sandbox's own cluster, then asked Postgres how many of them it still considers dead weight.
The answer came back exactly that many, straight from the engine's own bookkeeping, not a guess.
Only once I ran the cleanup command did that number drop. Deleting a row and reclaiming its space are two separate events.
Here's what actually surprised me.
I updated three hundred rows one way, and the table's own index never grew by a single byte. Updated the same rows a different way, and it doubled.
Same table, same row count, same number of updates. The only difference was which column I touched.
Picture a table that keeps getting bigger, and nobody can point to a slow query or a bad plan.
Autovacuum's logs show it running right on schedule. So what's actually stopping it from doing its job?
Just sit with that.
It's not falling behind. That's the instinct, because load is usually the answer to why something's slow.
But a vacuum that runs and reclaims nothing isn't broken. It's being careful.
Something, somewhere, is still holding onto a view of the table old enough that today's cleanup isn't safe yet.

tolerated.line: Something, somewhere, is still holding onto a view of the table old enough that today's cleanup isn't safe yet.

lines.text: So what actually holds that view open? Postgres's own documentation names exactly three things.
A transaction somebody forgot to close. A two phase commit left half finished. A replica's slot nobody dropped after that replica was decommissioned.
Three completely different situations, and from the cleanup job's point of view, they look identical.

tolerated.line: So what actually holds that view open? Postgres's own documentation names exactly three things.
A transaction somebody forgot to close. A two phase commit left half finished. A replica's slot nobody dropped after that replica was decommissioned.

lines.text: I made that invisible thing visible by holding one transaction open on purpose.
Six hundred updates landed on the same table while it sat there. I ran the cleanup command anyway, mid experiment, just to see.
It ran. It finished without error. It reclaimed not one of those six hundred dead rows, until I let that transaction go.
So how does autovacuum actually decide when to show up, if not on a timer?
It watches one number per table: how many rows changed since the last pass, measured against a threshold built from that table's own size.
Cross it, and a worker starts. There's no clock involved at all, which is exactly why 'it just ran an hour ago' tells you nothing.
Here's the part that makes all of this matter beyond disk space.
Postgres identifies every transaction with a number that eventually runs out and wraps back around to the start, like a clock face.
Freezing a row is what makes that safe — it tells Postgres, permanently, that this row is always in the past, no matter where the clock hand is.

Skip that for long enough, and Postgres doesn't corrupt your data. It simply refuses to take another write. Sentry's own production database did exactly that, for most of a working day, back in twenty fifteen.

lines.text: So pull all of that together.
A dead row nobody reclaimed. A table that keeps growing for no visible reason. A whole cluster that one day just stops accepting writes.
Different scales, same root cause every time: something nobody's watching is holding a horizon open.

tolerated.line: A dead row nobody reclaimed. A table that keeps growing for no visible reason. A whole cluster that one day just stops accepting writes.

lines.text: Last one. Sentry's database just hit that wall and stopped taking writes.
Somebody on the team suggests the obvious fix: turn autovacuum off so it quits interfering with recovery.
Before I tell you what they actually did, ask yourself whether that suggestion even makes sense.

tolerated.line: Last one. Sentry's database just hit that wall and stopped taking writes.
Somebody on the team suggests the obvious fix: turn autovacuum off so it quits interfering with recovery.

lines.text: Sentry's own writeup calls that exact suggestion out by name, because it's what everybody reaches for first.
It's backwards. Autovacuum isn't the thing fighting you during a wraparound crisis — it's the only thing capable of digging you out of one.
What actually worked was finding what was pinning the cleanup, giving the vacuum already running room to finish, and only then fixing the settings that let it get this bad.
